Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let
$1\le p\le\infty$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and scalar
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$, the pullback $\widehat v:=v\circ F$ belongs to
$W^{r,p}(\widehat K)$. For $r\ge1$ its first weak derivatives satisfy
$$D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v=\sum_{i=1}^d A_{ij}(D_{x_i}v)\circ F,$$
and higher derivatives are obtained by applying this constant-matrix rule
repeatedly. In particular, for each $0\le m\le r$,
$$|\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat K)}\le C(d,m)\|A\|^m|\det A|^{-1/p}|v|_{W^{m,p}(K)},$$
where $|\det A|^{-1/p}:=1$ for $p=\infty$. The reverse estimate holds
with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1<p<\infty$ and $p'=p/(p-1)$. For each facet $F$ of
$\widehat S_d$, restriction of smooth functions extends uniquely to a
bounded linear trace map
$$\gamma_F:W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)\to L^p(F;\mathbb R).$$
For real-valued $u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)$ and
$G\in W^{1,p'}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R^d)$, the facet traces satisfy
$$\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,\operatorname{div}G+\nabla u\cdot G\,dx =\sum_{F\subset\partial\widehat S_d}\int_F\gamma_Fu\,\gamma_FG\cdot\widehat n_F\,dS.$$
Here $\gamma_FG$ is the componentwise trace and $\widehat n_F$ is the
outward unit normal. The bounded C1-domain trace and Green theorems are not
used for the simplex.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nondegenerate affine $d$-simplex and let
$G\in C^1(\overline K;\mathbb R^d)$. If $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit
normal on each facet $F$, then
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$
For an orientation-preserving affine map $F_K(\widehat x)=b+A\widehat x$,
the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p<\infty$, and let
$\widehat S_d$ be the reference simplex. Then restrictions of functions
smooth on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\widehat S_d}$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)$ in its Sobolev norm. No density assertion for
$p=\infty$ is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Define the physical traces by $\gamma_Fu(F_K(\widehat x))=\gamma_{\widehat F}\widehat u(\widehat x)$ and $\gamma_FG(F_K(\widehat x))=(\det B)^{-1}B\gamma_{\widehat F}\widehat G(\widehat x)$. The reference traces in [F3] are in $L^2(\widehat F)$; the constant affine surface Jacobian $\det(B)|B^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}|>0$ from [F4] and the fixed matrix factor show these definitions give bounded $L^2(F)$ traces. For a fixed map, [F5] supplies smooth approximants to $\widehat u$ and each component of $G\circ F_K$; the reverse estimate in [F2] maps them to smooth approximants on $K$. Thus smooth functions on $K$ are dense in $W^{1,2}(K)$, and any two bounded affine-transfer trace maps agree on this dense smooth class, so they agree on all of $W^{1,2}(K)$.

Applying the componentwise weak chain rule [F2] and the identity $\sum_jB_{\ell j}(B^{-1})_{ji}=\delta_{\ell i}$ gives $\operatorname{div}_{\widehat x}\widehat G=\det(B)(\operatorname{div}_xG)\circ F_K$. Also $
abla_{\widehat x}\widehat u\cdot\widehat G=((B^T
abla_xu)\circ F_K)\cdot(\det(B)B^{-1}(G\circ F_K))=\det(B)(
abla_xu\cdot G)\circ F_K$. The volume products are integrable by [F7], so [F6] applied to their positive and negative parts identifies the reference volume integral in [F3] with the physical volume integral in the claim. The reference boundary products are integrable by [F3] and [F7]. By the trace definition in step 1.1, $\gamma_{\widehat F}\widehat G=\det(B)B^{-1}(\gamma_FG)\circ F_K$; hence its normal pairing is $\det(B)(\gamma_FG)\cdot B^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S=(\gamma_FG)\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS$ by [F4], while the scalar trace is the pullback of $\gamma_Fu$. Applying [F3] and summing over the finitely many facets proves the identity.

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev notation below. Each cell $K$ is the closed simplex from [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]; in $W^{m,2}(K)$ notation, $K$ means its open interior, and its facets are the boundary faces of that interior. Write $H^m(K):=W^{m,2}(K;\mathbb R)$ for $m=1,2$. Use the mesh and jump convention of [[def-sipdg-jump-average-convention]]. Specialize [[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]] to scalar real polynomials of a fixed degree $k\ge1$, so $V_h^{\rm br}=\prod_{K\in\mathcal T}\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R)$. On every cell $K$, let $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be a constant symmetric matrix. Assume common bounds $0<\lambda\le\Lambda<\infty$ such that
$$\lambda|\xi|^2\le \xi^TA_K\xi\le\Lambda|\xi|^2\qquad(\xi\in\mathbb R^d,\ K\in\mathcal T).$$
Write $A|_K=A_K$, let $h_F:=\operatorname{diam}(F)>0$, and fix a penalty parameter $\gamma>0$. Define $\mathcal D_h$ to consist of broken real-valued functions $v$ with $v|_K\in H^1(K)$, distributional $\operatorname{div}(A_K\nabla v|_K)\in L^2(K)$, and an $L^2(F)$ one-sided normal coefficient-flux trace $r_{K,F}(v)$ on every facet $F$ of each cell $K$. Precisely, $r_{K,F}(v)$ is the unique $L^2(F)$ function satisfying
$$\int_K A_K\nabla v\cdot\nabla\phi+\operatorname{div}(A_K\nabla v)\,\phi\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_F r_{K,F}(v)\,\gamma_F\phi\,dS\qquad(\phi\in C^\infty(\overline K)).$$
Here $\gamma_F\phi$ is the value trace from [[lem-sipdg-physical-simplex-trace-green]]; uniqueness follows by testing smooth functions supported near the relative interior of each facet, whose restrictions are dense in $L^2(F)$. If $F=K^-\cap K^+$ and $n_F$ points outward from $K^-$, set $q_F(v):=\tfrac12(r_{K^-,F}(v)-r_{K^+,F}(v))$; on a boundary facet set $q_F(v):=r_{K,F}(v)$ with the outward normal. These definitions agree with $\{A\nabla_hv\}_F\cdot n_F$ whenever the classical one-sided vector flux traces exist. Broken polynomials and cellwise $H^2$ functions belong to $\mathcal D_h$ by [[lem-sipdg-physical-simplex-trace-green]]. For $v,w\in\mathcal D_h$, define
$$a_h(v,w):=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T}\int_K A_K\nabla v\cdot\nabla w\,dx-\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h}\int_F q_F(v)[w]_F\,dS-\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h}\int_F q_F(w)[v]_F\,dS+\gamma\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h}h_F^{-1}\int_F[v]_F[w]_F\,dS,$$
All facet integrals and $L^2(F)$ norms use $(d-1)$-dimensional surface measure for the stated mesh dimension $d\ge2$. Counting measure is reserved for the separate one-dimensional interval examples in [[def-sipdg-jump-average-convention]]. The expression is real and symmetric.

Define the energy expression and its augmented version on $\mathcal D_h$ by
$$\|v\|_{DG}^2:=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T}\int_K A_K\nabla v\cdot\nabla v\,dx+\gamma\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h}h_F^{-1}\|[v]_F\|_{L^2(F)}^2,$$
$$\|v\|_{DG,*}^2:=\|v\|_{DG}^2+\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h}h_F\|q_F(v)\|_{L^2(F)}^2.$$
The first expression is initially a seminorm on $V_h^{\rm br}$; its definiteness is not part of this definition. The stated Sobolev notation follows [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. Cellwise $H^2$ functions have the required value and normal coefficient-flux traces by [[lem-sipdg-physical-simplex-trace-green]], because $A_K$ is constant. The augmented expression is defined whenever $v\in\mathcal D_h$, so it applies in particular to the exact functions, dual functions and discrete polynomials used below.

For $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ define the discrete load $\ell_h(w):=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T}\int_K f w\,dx$. A symmetric interior-penalty DG solution is a function $u_h\in V_h^{\rm br}$ satisfying $a_h(u_h,w_h)=\ell_h(w_h)$ for every $w_h\in V_h^{\rm br}$.

there is a constant independent of cell size such that, for every
$v\in\mathbb P_k(K)$ and every facet $F\subset\partial K$,
$$|v|_{W^{\ell,p}(K)} \le C h_K^{m-\ell+d(1/p-1/q)}|v|_{W^{m,q}(K)},$$

Use $1/\infty=0$. Constants may depend on $d,k,p,q$ and the family shape
regularity bound, but not on $K$ or $h_K$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.
